title: Point probability of zero in continuous vs discrete distributions
scenario_markdown: A systems engineer compares two operational variables: (1) $Y$, the daily server incident count modeled as a discrete Poisson random variable ($Y \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 5)$), and (2) $X$, the server reboot duration in minutes modeled as a continuous random variable with probability density function $f(x)$.
assumptions: Continuous random variables have continuous cumulative distribution functions where the area over a single point is zero
Discrete random variables assign positive probability mass P(Y = y) to individual points in their support

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: for continuous X, P(X = c) = 0 exactly because integral from c to c is 0. Density f(c) > 0 is not probability. For discrete Y, P(Y = 5) = 0.1755 > 0 via POISSON.DIST(5, 5, FALSE).

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the exact probability that reboot duration $X$ equals precisely $5.000\dots$ minutes ($P(X = 5)$)?

options.text_markdown: $P(X = 5) = 0$ exactly, because probability for a continuous variable is area under the density curve, and a single point has zero width: $\int_5^5 f(x)\,dx = 0$.
$P(X = 5) = f(5) > 0$, equal to the height of the probability density function at $x = 5$.
options.hint_markdown: Probability density $f(x)$ is not a probability; probability requires multiplying density by a non-zero interval width $dx$.

options.text_markdown: $P(X = 5)$ is extremely small (such as $0.0001$) but strictly greater than zero.
options.hint_markdown: In standard probability theory, the probability of any specific single real value for a continuous random variable is strictly 0.

stages.explanation_markdown: For any continuous random variable $X$, the probability of taking on any specific exact value is zero: $P(X = c) = 0$. Probabilities are computed over intervals as integrals $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Even though a reboot of 5 minutes is possible, observing exactly $5.000000\dots$ with infinite precision has probability zero.

stages.prompt_markdown: In contrast, what is the probability that daily incident count $Y$ equals exactly $5$ ($P(Y = 5)$) for $Y \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 5)$?

options.text_markdown: $P(Y = 5) = \frac{e^{-5} 5^5}{5!} \approx 0.1755 > 0$, because discrete distributions concentrate probability mass at individual integer points.
$P(Y = 5) = 0$, because individual points always carry zero probability.
options.hint_markdown: The $P(X = c) = 0$ rule applies only to continuous random variables. Discrete random variables have probability mass functions where individual outcomes have positive probability.
Use the Poisson PMF formula $P(Y = k) = e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k / k!$ or Excel `=POISSON.DIST(5, 5, FALSE)`.

stages.explanation_markdown: Discrete random variables have probability mass functions (PMF) that assign non-zero probability to specific integer values: $P(Y = 5) = \frac{e^{-5} 5^5}{5!} \approx 0.1755$ (Excel formula: `=POISSON.DIST(5, 5, FALSE)`). Unlike continuous variables, discrete individual outcomes have positive probability.

stages.prompt_markdown: Because $P(X = c) = 0$ for every single point in a continuous distribution, how are meaningful non-zero probabilities obtained for $X$?

options.text_markdown: By defining probability over an interval $[a, b]$ as the area under the density curve: $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
By summing the probabilities of all individual points in the range.
options.hint_markdown: There are uncountably many points in any continuous interval; summing zeros yields zero, which is why integration of density is required.

options.text_markdown: By multiplying the point density height by the total sample size $n$.
options.hint_markdown: Probability is intrinsic to the distribution and represents area under the curve, independent of sample size.

stages.explanation_markdown: For continuous random variables, probabilities exist only for intervals, representing the area under the density curve: $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. The total area under $f(x)$ across $(-\infty, \infty)$ is always exactly $1$.
